title: When fair dealing between shareholders breaks down
subtitle: Unfair prejudice petitions under s 994 and the buy-out remedy
objectives: State the s 994 petition test, including who may petition and the meaning of conduct 'unfairly prejudicial' to members' interests
Explain how legitimate expectations can arise in a quasi-partnership company, applying the O'Neill v Phillips framework
Apply the unfair prejudice test to a fact pattern and identify the likely remedy, including how a buy-out order is typically valued

leadingAuthorities.role: The statutory unfair prejudice petition, and the court's wide remedial discretion, including the standard buy-out order
Leading House of Lords authority on when unfairness arises from a broken legitimate expectation, not from formal legal rights alone

leadingAuthorities.citation: Re Saul D Harrison & Sons plc [1995] 1 BCLC 14
leadingAuthorities.role: Hoffmann LJ's framing of unfairness as tied to the company's constitution, agreements and understandings, not free-floating notions of fairness

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Lesson 10 dealt with wrongs done to the company itself. This lesson deals with something different: conduct that may be entirely lawful under the articles, yet still unfairly damages one shareholder's interests — often in a small company where the shareholders once trusted each other and no longer do. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can define unfair prejudice — this lesson checks whether you can spot a genuine legitimate expectation in a messy set of facts.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards scenario questions that require you to separate a genuine broken understanding from an ordinary business disagreement.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and fix the s 994 test itself before moving on — the legitimate expectation material in Parts 3 and 4 only makes sense once you know what 'unfairly prejudicial' has to mean in the first place.

overview.hook: Two friends start a small company together, each holding half the shares, each expecting to work in the business and share in its profits for as long as they both want to. Years later, one of them is voted off the board by the other, using votes that are entirely valid under the articles. Nothing unlawful has happened, on paper. And yet the excluded shareholder has a real claim — because in a company built on personal trust rather than pure capital, the law asks a harder question than 'was this technically permitted?'

parts.heading: Why Foss v Harbottle isn't the end of the story
parts.voice: structural — orients students before the detail arrives
body: Lesson 10 showed that Foss v Harbottle blocks an individual shareholder from suing for a wrong done to the company, absent the narrow statutory derivative-claim gateway. But not every shareholder grievance is a wrong done to the company at all. Sometimes the complaint is that the majority has run the company in a way that damages this particular shareholder's own interests as a member — excluding them from management, paying themselves excessive remuneration instead of dividends, or diluting their shareholding through an improperly motivated share issue.

Parliament created a separate remedy for exactly this situation. Section 994 of the Companies Act 2006 allows a member to petition the court on the ground that the company's affairs are being, have been, or are proposed to be conducted in a manner that is unfairly prejudicial to the interests of members generally, or of some part of the members (including at least the petitioner). This is a personal remedy belonging to the shareholder, not a derivative claim brought on the company's behalf — it doesn't need to overcome Foss v Harbottle at all, because it isn't suing for a wrong to the company in the first place.

The remedy is strikingly flexible by design: s 996 gives the court the widest possible discretion to make 'such order as it thinks fit' to give relief, and in practice one remedy dominates almost every successful petition — an order requiring the majority to buy the petitioner's shares at a fair price.

components.definition: A personal claim under s 994 by a member alleging the company's affairs have been conducted in a way that unfairly prejudices their interests as a member — distinct from a derivative claim, because it does not require overcoming Foss v Harbottle at all.

interaction.prompt: Is a s 994 unfair prejudice petition a derivative claim brought on the company's behalf, or a personal claim brought by the member?
options: A personal claim by the member
A derivative claim requiring permission under ss 260-264
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. An unfair prejudice petition is the member's own personal claim about how the company's affairs have affected their interests — it doesn't need the derivative-claim permission procedure at all.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: A s 994 petition is a personal claim belonging to the member, not a claim brought on the company's behalf. That's exactly why it doesn't need to clear the Foss v Harbottle/derivative-claim permission hurdles covered in Lesson 10.

parts.heading: Section 994: the statutory test
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Section 994(1) sets the test in a single, carefully worded sentence: a member may apply to the court by petition for an order on the ground that the company's affairs are being or have been conducted in a manner that is unfairly prejudicial to the interests of members generally or of some part of its members (including at least himself), or that an actual or proposed act or omission of the company is or would be so prejudicial.

Three elements repay close reading. First, 'unfairly prejudicial' is a composite phrase — conduct must be both prejudicial (damaging to the member's interests) and unfair (objectionable by some recognised standard), and neither word alone is enough. Second, the conduct is judged against the interests of members, not simply against strict legal rights; a member can be unfairly prejudiced by conduct that is entirely intra vires and consistent with the articles, which is precisely why the doctrine developed the legitimate expectation reasoning covered in Parts 3 and 4. Third, the petition can be brought over conduct 'proposed', not only conduct already carried out, allowing a member to head off prejudice before it happens.

Section 996 then supplies the remedy: the court may make such order as it thinks fit, and s 996(2) lists examples without limiting the court's discretion, including regulating the company's future conduct, requiring the company to do or refrain from doing an act, authorising civil proceedings, and — the remedy that dominates practice — providing for the purchase of the shares of any member by other members or by the company itself.

components.text: (1) A member of a company may apply to the court by petition for an order under this Part on the ground (a) that the company's affairs are being or have been conducted in a manner that is unfairly prejudicial to the interests of members generally or of some part of its members (including at least himself), or (b) that an actual or proposed act or omission of the company (including an act or omission on its behalf) is or would be so prejudicial.
elements: Available to a member, on their own petition, not as a derivative claim
Conduct must be both prejudicial and unfair — a composite test, not two alternatives
Judged by reference to members' interests, not strict legal rights alone
Covers conduct already carried out or merely proposed

interaction.prompt: Under s 994(1), why is it not enough for a petitioner to show conduct was simply 'prejudicial' to their interests?
options: Because the statutory test is a composite one — the conduct must be both prejudicial and unfair, and neither element alone satisfies it
Because s 994 only applies to conduct that breaches the articles of association
Because prejudice must be shown to every member of the company, not just the petitioner
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. 'Unfairly prejudicial' is a composite phrase — damage to the member's interests (prejudice) has to be combined with some recognised unfairness in how it came about, which is why the legitimate expectation case law matters so much.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Section 994 does not reduce to a single element. The conduct must be shown to be both prejudicial (damaging) and unfair (objectionable by a recognised standard) — that composite structure is exactly why the case law on legitimate expectations developed.

parts.heading: Re Saul D Harrison: unfairness measured against what the parties actually agreed
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Re Saul D Harrison & Sons plc gives the framework that shapes everything that follows in this lesson. A shareholder in a family textile company complained that the directors were running a failing business too conservatively, refusing to sell assets or wind it up, to her disadvantage as a shareholder wanting a return. Her petition failed — but the judgment matters far more for its reasoning than its outcome.

Hoffmann LJ explained that 'unfairness' in s 994 cannot mean whatever a judge personally thinks is unfair in the abstract. It has to be assessed against a background of rules the shareholders have actually agreed to — principally the company's articles, but also any collateral agreements, understandings or courses of dealing between the shareholders that equity would recognise as qualifying how the strict legal rights in the articles should be exercised. Conduct that is entirely consistent with the articles is not unfair merely because a minority shareholder dislikes the outcome — unless the shareholders' relationship carries an equitable understanding going beyond the bare articles.

This is why 'legitimate expectation' became the organising concept in unfair prejudice law: it names the equitable overlay — the promise, understanding or course of dealing — that can make strict reliance on legal rights under the articles unfair in the particular relationship between these particular shareholders, even though nothing in the articles has technically been breached.

components.caseName: Re Saul D Harrison & Sons plc
components.factsShort: A minority shareholder in a family company complained that a conservative business strategy she disagreed with was unfairly prejudicial to her interests.
components.ratioShort: Unfairness under s 994 is assessed against the company's constitution and any collateral agreements or understandings between the shareholders, not against a judge's free-standing sense of fairness.

expanded.facts: The petitioner held a minority stake in a family textile company that had fallen on hard times. She wanted the directors (family members with majority control) to sell the company's assets or wind it up to realise value for shareholders, but the directors preferred to continue trading conservatively in the hope of a turnaround, consistently with their powers under the articles.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Hoffmann LJ held that a member's statutory rights (broadly, to have the company's affairs conducted in accordance with the articles) generally correspond to the rights he enjoys as a shareholder under general company law. Whether conduct is unfair has to be tested against those rules and understandings, not against a general standard of commercial fairness the court invents for the occasion; conduct which is exactly in accordance with the articles will usually not be unfair, unless equity would recognise some further restriction going beyond the strict letter of the articles.
expanded.significance: This judgment supplies the analytical framework the rest of unfair prejudice law builds on. It shifts the inquiry from 'was this outcome fair in the abstract' to 'what did these shareholders actually agree to, expressly or by understanding' — precisely the groundwork O'Neill v Phillips builds on to define when a legitimate expectation arises.

interaction.prompt: In this passage adapted from Re Saul D Harrison, highlight the sentence that states the ratio on how unfairness should be assessed.
interaction.passage: Counsel for the petitioner argued that the directors' conservative strategy was simply unfair to a shareholder wanting a return on her investment. The Court of Appeal rejected the submission that unfairness could be judged in the abstract. Whether conduct is unfairly prejudicial must be tested against the rules the shareholders have actually agreed to, principally the articles of association, together with any collateral understanding equity would recognise as qualifying the strict exercise of rights under them. Conduct exactly in accordance with the articles will generally not be unfair absent some further such understanding.
interaction.ratioSentence: Whether conduct is unfairly prejudicial must be tested against the rules the shareholders have actually agreed to, principally the articles of association, together with any collateral understanding equity would recognise as qualifying the strict exercise of rights under them.

parts.heading: O'Neill v Phillips: when does a legitimate expectation actually arise?
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the hard question before resolving it
body: Re Saul D Harrison tells you where to look for unfairness. O'Neill v Phillips tells you exactly when a legitimate expectation crystallises, and it does so through facts every company law examiner returns to. Mr O'Neill worked his way up in Mr Phillips's construction company, was given 25% of the shares and made a director, and — informally, in discussions about the company's future — Mr Phillips indicated O'Neill might one day receive an equal 50% share and profit split. That equal split was never formally implemented. When the company hit financial difficulty and the relationship soured, Phillips resumed sole control, and O'Neill petitioned, claiming his expectation of eventual equality had been unfairly defeated.

The House of Lords dismissed the petition. Lord Hoffmann held that a legitimate expectation does not arise merely because informal, hopeful discussions took place about a shareholder's future position — it requires something amounting to an equitable obligation, typically arising from a promise or a course of dealing on which the shareholder could reasonably rely as more than a mere aspiration. Because the 50% arrangement had never moved beyond discussion to something the parties actually treated as binding, no legitimate expectation had crystallised, and Phillips was entitled to fall back on his strict legal rights under the articles.

The judgment also supplies a practical formula worth remembering: a member will generally not be able to complain of unfairness unless there has been some breach of the terms on which they agreed the affairs of the company should be conducted — whether that agreement is found in the articles, in a separate agreement, or in a course of dealing the law will treat as generating an equitable restraint. Read together with Saul D Harrison, O'Neill confirms that legitimate expectations are the exception in shareholder relationships, not the default — they need to be earned through something more concrete than hope.

components.label: What does and doesn't create a legitimate expectation
points: Does — an express or clearly implied promise the parties genuinely treated as binding, not merely aspirational
Does — a settled course of dealing consistent only with an understanding beyond the strict articles (classic in a genuine quasi-partnership company)
Does not — informal discussion of a hoped-for future arrangement that was never implemented or treated as binding
Does not — a shareholder's unilateral hope or expectation, however genuinely held, without some equitable obligation on the other side

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact from the O'Neill v Phillips scenario that was decisive in the House of Lords finding no legitimate expectation had crystallised.
interaction.scenarioText: O'Neill was given 25% of the shares and made a director. In informal discussions about the company's future, Phillips indicated O'Neill might one day receive an equal 50% share and profit split. That equal arrangement was never formally implemented before the relationship soured.
tappableSpans: given 25% of the shares and made a director
informal discussions about the company's future
indicated O'Neill might one day receive an equal 50% share
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The 50% arrangement stayed at the level of hopeful discussion and was never implemented or treated by the parties as a binding understanding — which is exactly why Lord Hoffmann held no legitimate expectation had crystallised, however genuine O'Neill's hope had been.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The decisive fact isn't the existence of the 25% shareholding or the discussions themselves — it's that the 50% arrangement was never actually implemented or treated as binding. That gap between hope and a real, relied-upon understanding is what O'Neill turns on.

parts.heading: The remedy: buy-out orders and how shares are valued
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Once unfair prejudice is established, s 996's remedial discretion is genuinely wide, but in the overwhelming majority of successful petitions the court makes a share purchase order: requiring the other shareholders, or the company itself, to buy the petitioner's shares at a fair value, so the petitioner can exit the company with their investment realised rather than remaining trapped as a minority in a relationship that has broken down.

Two valuation questions recur in problem questions. First, should the shares be valued pro rata (as a straightforward proportion of the whole company's value) or with a discount applied for being a minority holding? Courts in quasi-partnership cases generally favour a pro-rata valuation without a minority discount, on the reasoning that the petitioner is only leaving because of the respondent's unfair conduct, and should not additionally be penalised in the price for holding a minority stake they never chose to be forced out of. Second, at what date should the shares be valued — the date of the petition, the date of the unfairly prejudicial conduct, or the date of trial? Courts have flexibility here and will choose whichever date avoids the valuation itself being distorted by the very conduct complained of, often the date immediately before the unfair conduct began.

Distinguishing a genuine quasi-partnership from an ordinary company matters throughout this analysis. A quasi-partnership typically shows some combination of: a small number of shareholders who are also directors, a business built on personal relationships and mutual trust rather than pure capital investment, restrictions on the free transfer of shares, and an understanding (express or by course of dealing) that all shareholder-directors would participate in management. Only in that kind of company does the O'Neill-style legitimate expectation reasoning tend to bite; a shareholder in a large, arm's-length company with freely tradeable shares will usually be limited to their strict legal rights under the articles.

components.text: (1) If the court is satisfied that a petition under this Part is well founded, it may make such order as it thinks fit for giving relief in respect of the matters complained of. (2) Without prejudice to the generality of subsection (1), the court's order may... provide for the purchase of the shares of any members of the company by other members or by the company itself.
elements: Court's discretion is very wide — 'such order as it thinks fit'
Statute expressly contemplates a share purchase order as one option among several
In practice, the buy-out order dominates successful petitions
Valuation typically favours no minority discount and a date that isn't distorted by the unfair conduct itself

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is the stronger candidate for a s 994 petition based on a legitimate expectation?
interaction.scenarioA: Three friends found a small company, each holding a third of the shares, all working as directors from the outset, with an unwritten but consistently followed understanding that each would remain a director and share equally in profits for as long as they all wished to work in the business. One is later excluded from management and decision-making by the other two.
interaction.scenarioB: A shareholder in a large public company, holding a small, freely tradeable stake, is unhappy that the board's dividend policy favours reinvestment over payouts, exactly as the articles and published dividend policy permit.
interaction.explanation: A shows the hallmarks of a genuine quasi-partnership — small number of shareholder-directors, mutual trust, a consistent course of dealing going beyond the bare articles — exactly the setting where O'Neill-style legitimate expectations arise. B is an ordinary large-company shareholder objecting to conduct that is entirely consistent with the articles and no more than an investment decision they dislike, which Saul D Harrison confirms is not unfair.

testPool.prompt: Name the two-word composite test at the heart of s 994(1).
testPool.modelAnswer: Conduct must be 'unfairly prejudicial' to the interests of members generally or of some part of the members — a composite test requiring both unfairness and prejudice.

testPool.prompt: Put the events of O'Neill v Phillips in the order they occurred.
items: O'Neill is given 25% of the shares and made a director
Phillips informally indicates O'Neill might one day receive an equal 50% share and profit split
The equal arrangement is never formally implemented
The company faces financial difficulty and the relationship deteriorates
O'Neill petitions under s 994, and the House of Lords finds no legitimate expectation had crystallised

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT, by itself, evidence of a company being a genuine quasi-partnership for unfair prejudice purposes?
options: A small number of shareholders who are also directors
Restrictions on the free transfer of shares
The company having a large number of employees on its payroll
testPool.trapExplanation: The size of a company's workforce says nothing about the relationship between its shareholders. Quasi-partnership indicators concern the shareholders' own relationship — small numbers, personal trust, transfer restrictions, mutual participation in management — not the scale of the business's operations.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that conduct which is entirely lawful and consistent with a company's articles can never amount to unfair prejudice under s 994?
sliderLabels: Confident — lawful conduct under the articles can never be unfair
Not confident — lawful conduct can still be unfair if it breaches a legitimate expectation
testPool.correctPosition: Not confident — lawful conduct can still be unfair if it breaches a legitimate expectation
testPool.explanation: Not confident is correct. Saul D Harrison and O'Neill v Phillips both confirm that conduct entirely within the articles can still be unfairly prejudicial where it breaches a legitimate expectation arising from a promise or course of dealing going beyond the bare articles.

testPool.prompt: A shareholder-director in a genuine quasi-partnership company is excluded from management by the other shareholder-directors, using votes that are entirely valid under the articles, breaking a long-standing mutual understanding that all shareholder-directors would participate in running the business. Is this likely to be unfairly prejudicial?
options: Yes — exclusion from management in breach of a legitimate expectation arising from the quasi-partnership understanding is a classic ground for a successful s 994 petition
No — because the votes used were entirely valid under the articles, the conduct cannot be unfair
No — unfair prejudice only applies to financial harm, not exclusion from management
testPool.explanation: Exclusion from management, in breach of a genuine quasi-partnership understanding, is one of the paradigm fact patterns for a successful unfair prejudice petition — Saul D Harrison and O'Neill together confirm that formal validity under the articles does not answer the fairness question where a legitimate expectation has been breached.

testPool.prompt: Amara and Tobias founded Larkspur Interiors Ltd together, each holding 50% of the shares and both working as directors, with a consistent seven-year understanding that both would run the business and share profits equally. After a disagreement, Tobias uses a shareholders' agreement clause (of doubtful application here) to attempt to remove Amara as a director and stop paying her any return, while continuing to draw his own director's salary. Analyse whether Amara has a viable s 994 petition, and the likely remedy.
factsToOrder: Amara and Tobias each hold 50% and have both worked as directors for seven years
A consistent understanding existed that both would run the business and share profits equally
Tobias removes Amara as a director and stops her returns, while continuing to pay himself
The clause relied on by Tobias is of doubtful application to these facts

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Amara can bring a successful s 994 petition against Tobias, and what remedy she is likely to obtain.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 994 requires conduct unfairly prejudicial to the petitioner's interests as a member. Unfairness is assessed against the company's constitution and any collateral understanding equity would recognise (Saul D Harrison), and a legitimate expectation can arise from a consistent course of dealing in a genuine quasi-partnership, even absent formal implementation (O'Neill v Phillips). The standard remedy is a share purchase order under s 996, typically valued pro rata without a minority discount.
modelAnswer.application: Larkspur shows the hallmarks of a genuine quasi-partnership: two founder shareholder-directors, equal shares, and a consistent seven-year course of dealing that both would run the business and share profits equally. Tobias's exclusion of Amara from management and her returns, while continuing to pay himself, breaches that legitimate expectation — the doubtful applicability of the clause he relies on strengthens Amara's case that the conduct goes beyond his strict rights under any agreement. This mirrors the paradigm quasi-partnership exclusion case rather than O'Neill's facts, where no such settled understanding had crystallised.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Amara has a strong s 994 petition. The likely remedy is an order requiring Tobias to purchase her shares at a fair value, valued pro rata without a minority discount, at a date that is not distorted by his own unfairly prejudicial conduct.

testPool.prompt: In a successful s 994 petition arising from a genuine quasi-partnership, do courts typically apply a minority discount when valuing the petitioner's shares for a buy-out order?
options: No — a pro-rata valuation without a minority discount is typically applied
Yes — a minority discount is always applied regardless of the circumstances

testPool.prompt: Under s 996(2), which remedy is expressly contemplated by the statute and dominates practice in successful unfair prejudice petitions?
options: An order for the purchase of the petitioner's shares by other members or by the company
Automatic dissolution of the company
Criminal sanctions against the respondent directors

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from O'Neill v Phillips, highlight the sentence that states the general test for when a member can complain of unfairness.
testPool.passage: It was submitted that any disappointed hope about a shareholder's future position in the company should found a s 994 petition. Their Lordships rejected this. A member of a company will not ordinarily be entitled to complain of unfairness unless there has been some breach of the terms on which he agreed that the affairs of the company should be conducted, whether those terms are found in the articles, a separate agreement, or a course of dealing which equity treats as generating an obligation of fair dealing beyond the strict letter of the articles.
testPool.ratioSentence: A member of a company will not ordinarily be entitled to complain of unfairness unless there has been some breach of the terms on which he agreed that the affairs of the company should be conducted, whether those terms are found in the articles, a separate agreement, or a course of dealing which equity treats as generating an obligation of fair dealing beyond the strict letter of the articles.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly signals this company is a genuine quasi-partnership, rather than an ordinary capital-investment company.
testPool.scenarioText: Three former colleagues incorporated a design consultancy together. All three hold equal shares, all three are directors and work full-time in the business, shares cannot be transferred without the others' consent, and for nine years all three have shared profits equally by informal agreement rather than by any written shareholders' agreement.
tappableSpans: Three former colleagues incorporated a design consultancy together
all three are directors and work full-time in the business
shares cannot be transferred without the others' consent
nine years all three have shared profits equally by informal agreement
testPool.correctSpan: nine years all three have shared profits equally by informal agreement
testPool.explanation: While every fact here supports a quasi-partnership finding, the sustained nine-year course of dealing is what most directly supplies the O'Neill-style legitimate expectation — a settled practice the parties actually relied on, rather than a one-off structural feature like the transfer restriction or director status alone.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario most closely mirrors O'Neill v Phillips itself, rather than a paradigm successful quasi-partnership petition?
testPool.scenarioA: A shareholder was given informal, non-binding indications during discussions that they might one day receive a larger stake, but that arrangement was never implemented before the relationship broke down.
testPool.scenarioB: A shareholder who has co-managed a small company on an equal footing with the other founder for a decade, under a consistent understanding of equal participation, is suddenly excluded from all management decisions.
testPool.explanation: A mirrors O'Neill v Phillips precisely: a hoped-for future arrangement that was discussed but never implemented, which the House of Lords held did not crystallise into a legitimate expectation. B is the paradigm successful petition — a settled, long-standing course of dealing that was actually relied upon and then broken.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures the relationship between Re Saul D Harrison and O'Neill v Phillips?
options: Saul D Harrison establishes that unfairness must be assessed against the shareholders' actual agreed rules and understandings; O'Neill v Phillips then specifies what kind of understanding is required for a legitimate expectation to crystallise, and confirms informal, unimplemented discussion is not enough
O'Neill v Phillips overruled Saul D Harrison and replaced its test entirely
The two cases address unrelated areas of company law with no meaningful connection
testPool.trapExplanation: Neither wrong option reflects the actual relationship. O'Neill did not overrule Saul D Harrison — it builds directly on its framework, refining exactly what kind of promise or course of dealing is needed for a legitimate expectation to arise.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court works through when analysing a s 994 petition based on an alleged legitimate expectation.
items: Identify the company's constitution and any collateral agreements or course of dealing
Assess whether a genuine legitimate expectation arose beyond mere hope or informal discussion
Determine whether the respondent's conduct breached that expectation
If unfairly prejudicial conduct is established, consider the appropriate remedy under s 996

testPool.prompt: A court finds unfair prejudice and orders a buy-out of the petitioner's shares. The company's value has fallen significantly since the unfairly prejudicial conduct began, largely because of that same conduct. At which date is the court most likely to value the shares?
options: A date reflecting the company's value before the unfairly prejudicial conduct distorted it, rather than a later, depressed value
Always the date of the trial, regardless of the cause of any fall in value
Always the date the company was incorporated
testPool.explanation: Courts have flexibility over the valuation date precisely so the petitioner isn't penalised by a fall in value caused by the very unfair conduct complained of — choosing a date before that conduct took effect is the typical, fairer approach in this situation.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is assuming that conduct valid under the articles can never be unfair. Saul D Harrison and O'Neill v Phillips together establish the opposite: strict legal validity is the starting point, not the end point, and a genuine legitimate expectation — arising from a real promise or settled course of dealing, never mere hope — can make otherwise lawful conduct unfairly prejudicial.
